title: Vitello Tonnato
subtitle: Cold roasted veal with a tuna and caper sauce
excerpt: The great Piedmontese antipasto: veal shoulder poached or roasted then thinly sliced and blanketed in a smooth, creamy sauce made from tinned tuna, anchovies, capers, and mayonnaise. Served cold, it is one of the most elegant cold dishes in Italian cooking.

recipe.sourceNotes: Vitello tonnato is a Piedmontese dish that has spread throughout northern Italian cooking and become one of the most widely served antipasti at Italian summer tables and restaurants. The combination of veal and tuna is counterintuitive to non-Italian cooks but deeply established in the culinary tradition of Piedmont, where the dish appears in cookbooks from the late eighteenth century. The veal provides a neutral, delicate base; the tuna sauce adds richness and an oceanic depth that cuts through the mildness of the meat. The modern version of the sauce, enriched with mayonnaise to produce a smooth, creamy coating, became standard in the twentieth century. The dish must be served cold and is traditionally made the day before: the veal absorbs the sauce and the flavours meld overnight.

recipeTools.notes: A saucepan large enough to submerge the veal.

content.text: Poach the veal very gently, barely simmering, so it stays moist and pale: aggressive boiling toughens the meat and makes it fibrous. Cool the veal completely in its poaching liquid before slicing: warm veal tears rather than slices cleanly. Slice very thinly, about 3 mm, for the best texture and presentation. The sauce improves on standing; make it at least a few hours ahead.

items.preparation: boned and rolled, tied with string
1 tin, drained; good-quality tuna in olive oil

content.text: Place the veal in a snug saucepan with the onion, carrot, celery, bay, thyme, and white wine. Cover with cold water. Bring very slowly to a simmer and poach over the lowest heat for 50 to 60 minutes until the veal is just cooked through (a skewer should meet no resistance). Cool completely in the poaching liquid, then refrigerate until cold.

Make the sauce: blend the tuna, anchovies, capers, and lemon juice together with a hand blender until smooth. Fold in the mayonnaise. Taste: the sauce should be savoury, slightly salty, and sharply lemon-forward. Thin with a little of the poaching liquid if needed to reach a coating consistency.

Slice the cold veal very thinly. Arrange in a single layer (or slightly overlapping) on a large flat plate. Spoon the tuna sauce generously over the top to cover completely. Scatter with capers and parsley. Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours before serving, or overnight. Serve cold as a starter or summer main.
